pharmaTerms.title: In the pharmacy's terms
pharmaTerms.description: The glossary names what a pharmacy buyer asks about: NDC, formulary, drug shortage, recall class and days of supply. Here, supply risk means a shortage, a recall by the product's maker, or too few days of stock on hand.

pharmaAnswer.title: The answer in SQL
pharmaAnswer.description: The view product_risk joins each product's stock to its shortage, its manufacturer's ongoing recalls and its Medicaid prescriptions, and is kept stored. The critical products at risk come first, fewest days of supply first.

pharmaByRisk.title: By risk, in GraphQL
pharmaByRisk.description: The same view grouped by risk: how many products face a shortage, a recall or both, the stock they hold and how often Medicaid prescribes them.

pharmaRest.title: The same answer over REST
pharmaRest.description: The view is a REST endpoint too, grouped and summed on the server. Any client that speaks HTTP gets the answer without writing SQL.

pharmaRecap.title: What you saw
pharmaRecap.description: You saw the pharmacy's own data joined by NDC and by firm to public drug data, all in one governed model. One view answers which products are at risk, in SQL, GraphQL and REST, and each role sees only what it's allowed to.

storefrontScenario.title: One model, an app and BI
storefrontScenario.description: A coffee retailer serves two consumers from one model. Its app's order-history screen shows a signed-in customer their orders, and its BI tool charts revenue and late shipments for the analysts. The orders are in PostgreSQL: customers, orders and each order's lines.

storefrontCatalog.title: The catalog, in MongoDB
storefrontCatalog.description: Each product is a MongoDB document, with its name, category, price and picture. Provisa reads it as a table.

storefrontShipping.title: Shipping, over REST
storefrontShipping.description: Each order's shipment comes from the internal shipping service over REST, read through its OpenAPI document: the carrier, the tracking number, and when it was promised and delivered.

storefrontRelations.title: Relationships, declared once
storefrontRelations.description: OF_PRODUCT joins an order line in PostgreSQL to its product in MongoDB. With PLACED_BY, HAS_ITEM and SHIPPED_AS, these four relationships are declared once, and both the app and the BI tool read through them.

storefrontAsCustomer.title: Signed in as the customer
storefrontAsCustomer.description: The app sends its queries as the customer role, whose row filters limit every answer to the signed-in customer's own orders. Next, the role picker switches to customer, so the query below runs just as the app runs it.

storefrontScreen.title: The app's one query
storefrontScreen.description: The order-history screen sends this one nested GraphQL query: each order with its lines, each line's product from the catalog, and the order's shipment from the shipping service. Run as customer, it answers seven orders, all the signed-in customer's own.

storefrontApp.title: The screen it feeds
storefrontApp.description: This is the sample app's order-history screen, rendering that answer for the demo's signed-in customer: seven orders, their lines with product pictures from MongoDB, and delivery status from the shipping service. The app holds no joins and no access rules; the model holds both.

storefrontJsonApi.title: The same orders over JSON:API
storefrontJsonApi.description: A client that prefers JSON:API asks for the same orders, still as the customer, with their lines and shipments included. Each order links the lines and the shipment it includes, and a line's id is its composite key.

storefrontAnalyst.title: Now as the analyst
storefrontAnalyst.description: The BI side reads as analyst: it sees every order, but no customer's email. Next, the run-as picker switches to analyst.

storefrontAnalystSql.title: The analyst's SQL
storefrontAnalystSql.description: Late shipments by region and carrier, over the same tables and relationships. a_customer shows an email as the analyst reads it: masked.

storefrontBi.title: The BI dashboard
storefrontBi.description: Apache Superset connects over the PostgreSQL wire protocol, with the PostgreSQL dialect: host and port of Provisa's pgwire server (5439 by default), database provisa, user analyst. It browses the shop's tables and views and charts revenue by region and late shipments by carrier from the same model.

storefrontEveryRole.title: Back to every role
storefrontEveryRole.description: Next, the role picker switches back to All. The BI side reads as its own role, which is chosen where its SQL runs.

storefrontPoint.title: One model, two consumers
storefrontPoint.description: SHIPPED_AS joins an order to its shipment. The app and the BI tool both read through it and every other relationship, under the same rules: the customer sees their own orders, the analyst sees no emails. Change a relationship or a rule here, and both consumers have it. There is nothing to keep in sync.

hasuramigrationScenario.title: An app moving off Hasura
hasuramigrationScenario.description: An outfitter's storefront and support desk ran on Hasura v2 over this PostgreSQL database: customers, the catalog, orders and their lines, with roles for customers, support staff and analysts. The team moves the app to Provisa, and gains what Hasura could not give it: the sales team's Salesforce accounts beside the orders, under the same rules.

hasuramigrationImport.title: One import, and it works
hasuramigrationImport.description: Admin › Import read the app's Hasura metadata export and showed what it became before applying anything. Carried as it is: the tables, their custom names, every relationship, the select, insert, update and delete permissions as row rules, column grants and write grants. Mapped to a better Provisa feature, each saying why: the inherited role, the action as a command, the event trigger as a trigger on the table's changes, the session variable and the claim that supplies it. Redo by hand, each saying what to do: the computed field and the trigger retries.

hasuramigrationTables.title: The tables, as the app knew them
hasuramigrationTables.description: The four tables came over with the names the app uses. customers keeps Hasura's custom names givenName and familyName, the products table keeps its root name catalog, and each column carries the roles that may read it, from the select permissions.

hasuramigrationAsAna.title: Signed in as Ana
hasuramigrationAsAna.description: Ana is a customer. Her token carried x-hasura-user-id: 1, and Provisa reads that claim as the session value hasura_user_id, which the imported row rules compare against. Next, the role picker switches to ana, so the queries below run just as the storefront runs them for her.

hasuramigrationMyOrders.title: The order history, reshaped
hasuramigrationMyOrders.description: The storefront's order-history query, reshaped once for Provisa: the root field carries its domain, the column names follow Provisa's convention, and order_by is a list. The relationships items and product kept their Hasura names. Run as Ana, it answers her four orders and no one else's.

hasuramigrationProfile.title: A read by key
hasuramigrationProfile.description: Hasura's customers_by_pk becomes a filter on the table. The full_name computed field is just the two names the screen puts together, and the import listed it as one to redo by hand. The row rule still decides what Ana sees: only her own row.

hasuramigrationSalesforce.title: What Hasura couldn't do: Salesforce
hasuramigrationSalesforce.description: The sales team keeps its accounts in Salesforce. Provisa registers the org as a source and its Account object as a table. Each business customer in the store names the account it buys for.

hasuramigrationAccount.title: One more relationship
hasuramigrationAccount.description: BUYS_FOR joins a customer to their Salesforce account, approved like the relationships the import carried. From here the account is one field away from every customer, in every interface, under every role's rules.

hasuramigrationAsSupport.title: The support desk
hasuramigrationAsSupport.description: Support staff can read every order and every customer, as their Hasura permissions allowed. Next, the role picker switches to support, and the support desk's order screen runs as they run it.

hasuramigrationSupportScreen.title: Orders with their accounts
hasuramigrationSupportScreen.description: The support desk's order screen, reshaped, with something new: beside each order's customer, the account from Salesforce, its industry and city, in the same request. Customers without an account show none.

hasuramigrationAnalyst.title: The analyst
hasuramigrationAnalyst.description: Analysts can read order totals and account links, but no names or emails, and never cancelled orders. Those are the row rule and column lists the import carried over. Next, the role picker switches to analyst.

hasuramigrationByIndustry.title: Revenue by industry
hasuramigrationByIndustry.description: One SQL statement over the store and Salesforce: revenue by the industry of the account behind each order. The analyst's rules apply as they do in GraphQL: cancelled orders are left out, and no name or email is read.

hasuramigrationRecap.title: What you saw
hasuramigrationRecap.description: A Hasura app imported in one step and working at once: tables, names, relationships, roles, row rules, write permissions, the action and the triggers. The queries changed shape once; the rules did not change at all. And one relationship later, the app reads its Salesforce accounts beside its orders, with nothing to keep in sync.

reproduceScenario.title: What this demo is
reproduceScenario.description: A bank files an exposure report with its regulator for 30 September. The regulator asks where the rates desk's figure came from, and for the report exactly as it was filed: a rate has been corrected since. The bank's trading book is read live from its own database.

reproduceBook.title: The trading book
reproduceBook.description: Each position: its desk, its notional in its own currency and the rate it converts to USD at, valid from 30 September. One of these rates is corrected after the report is first filed.

reproduceLineage.title: Where the figure comes from
reproduceLineage.description: The report's exposure column, traced back: each desk's exposure is the sum of notional times fx_rate over its positions. Every column of the report leads to the source columns it is computed from.

reproduceRefreshes.title: The refreshes that built it
reproduceRefreshes.description: Each build of the report records what it was built from: the version of the report's definition, and the version of its input with how that was established. Two builds: one as first filed, one after the correction.

reproduceImpact.title: What a rename would break
reproduceImpact.description: Rename fx_rate here, and Provisa lists what reads it before you save: the report among them. Nothing that depends on a column changes without being named first.

reproduceNow.title: The report now
reproduceNow.description: Each desk's exposure as the report stands today, with when Provisa recorded each figure. The rates desk reads 1,550,000: the corrected rate.

reproduceAsOf.title: As of 30 September
reproduceAsOf.description: The report as of its business date: what the figures were for 30 September.

reproduceAsOfNow.title: As of 30 September, as recorded now
reproduceAsOfNow.description: Read as Provisa has it recorded today, 30 September shows the corrected figure: 1,550,000 for the rates desk. That is what the books say now, not what was filed.

reproduceAsFiled.title: As recorded when it was filed
reproduceAsFiled.description: This is the time the report was first built and filed, taken from the answer in the refreshes step. It falls after the filed figures were entered and before the correction was. The report is now read as Provisa had it recorded at that time, so nothing recorded later can change it.

reproduceFiled.title: The report as filed
reproduceFiled.description: As of 30 September and as recorded when it was filed: the rates desk reads 1,540,000, the figure the regulator received. The correction recorded since does not change what was filed.

reproduceAudit.title: Who read it, and as of when
reproduceAudit.description: The audit log records every read: who ran it, as which role, and the time it read the report as of and as recorded at. The regulator's reproduction is itself on record.

reproduceRecap.title: What you saw
reproduceRecap.description: One report, explained and reproduced: its figure traced to its source columns and the refresh that built it, the impact of a change named before it is made, the report as filed beside the report now, and every read of it in the audit log.

churnScenario.title: What this demo is
churnScenario.description: A subscription business wants to know which customers are about to cancel. Its customers and a year of their monthly usage are in its own database, and a data scientist trains a model on them in the browser.

churnCustomers.title: The customers
churnCustomers.description: Each customer's plan, region, tenure and the day they cancelled, if they have. Their email address is masked for the analyst role: it arrives as *** and its domain.

churnUsage.title: Their usage
churnUsage.description: Twelve months of each customer's sign-ins and support tickets, joined to the customer they belong to.

churnAnalyst.title: Read as the analyst
churnAnalyst.description: Next, the role picker switches to analyst, the role the data scientist reads with, so every surface after this runs as the analyst.

churnFeatures.title: The features the model learns from
churnFeatures.description: One row a customer: plan, tenure, sign-ins a month, tickets in the year, and whether they cancelled. A materialized view, built through the governed pipeline. The email addresses are masked, as the analyst is served them.

churnGraphql.title: The same features over GraphQL
churnGraphql.description: The demo's example query reads the same view as the analyst, with the same mask: every surface serves one governed answer.

churnNotebook.title: A model, trained in your browser
churnNotebook.description: The demo's notebook, run in the Notebook tab: the features read into pandas as the analyst, a scikit-learn model trained on them, and the customers most at risk listed. Python runs in your browser, and the email addresses are still masked.

churnEveryRole.title: Back to every role
churnEveryRole.description: Next, the role picker switches back to All.

churnRecap.title: What you saw
churnRecap.description: Governed data straight into a data scientist's notebook: the analyst's mask applied on the way in, and a model trained without the data leaving the browser. In a desktop Jupyter the same code reads large pulls over Arrow Flight. The churnprod demo puts this model in production.

dataroomIntro.title: A data room with no exports
dataroomIntro.description: Northfield Supply is selling itself, and each prospective buyer's clean team needs to see the business before it bids. Instead of exporting extracts into a data room, the seller connects Provisa to its own systems and gives each bidder governed access that ends on the deal date. Nothing is copied out, and no customer identity leaves the room. This is the order and finance system, a Postgres database read in place: 2,400 customers, their orders since 2023 and the invoice of each.

dataroomCrm.title: The CRM
dataroomCrm.description: The sales team's Salesforce: each business customer's account and its deals. Its rows are landed once into the room and read from there, so the bidders' questions never reach Salesforce.

dataroomInvite.title: Setting up the room: invite the analysts
dataroomInvite.description: On the seller's Users page, bidder A's two analysts are added as local accounts, each bound to the bidder_a role. They sign in to the seller's Provisa over HTTPS. A self-hosted seller exposes only HTTPS, through its own TLS edge (an ingress or reverse proxy with a public certificate), while the stores, the engine and the database protocols stay private; on hosted Provisa the org's own address already serves it. Nothing in this demo opens a port.

dataroomGrant.title: A grant that ends on the deal date
dataroomGrant.description: Each analyst's grant of bidder_a carries an end date: the deal date. From that moment the role is no longer theirs, on every request however it arrives. An account has no end date of its own; the grant's end ends the access.

dataroomSignedIn.title: What an analyst sees
dataroomSignedIn.description: Signed in, an analyst of bidder A sees what bidder_a is granted: the aggregate views, the profiles, the masked sample and the seller's records without a single customer identity. No customer's name, and no business or deal name from the CRM, is there to read.

dataroomBidder.title: Now as bidder A
dataroomBidder.description: The next statements run as bidder_a, exactly as the analysts' do.

dataroomProfile.title: The profile of the invoices
dataroomProfile.description: Each column of the invoices table as the profiler found it: its rows, nulls, distinct values and range. A bidder learns how complete the records are without reading one of them. Here, some invoices have never been paid.

dataroomCounts.title: Customer counts
dataroomCounts.description: How many customers each segment and region has, and how many ordered in the last twelve months. A count, never a customer.

dataroomAnswer.title: Revenue by segment
dataroomAnswer.description: Orders, revenue and the average order of each segment, by year, from the orders and the customers' segments.

dataroomPipeline.title: The sales pipeline
dataroomPipeline.description: The CRM's deals by industry and stage, with their value and their value weighted by the chance each closes. The businesses' and the deals' names stay in the CRM.

dataroomQuality.title: Data quality scores
dataroomQuality.description: Each check of the seller's records and how many rows fail it: customers with no email, phone numbers that are not ten digits, invoices never paid. The flaws a buyer looks for, counted.

dataroomSample.title: A masked sample
dataroomSample.description: One customer in fifty, as a bidder reads them: no name, the email's name part and the phone's digits masked. The shape of the data, never the person.

dataroomRefused.title: Customer names are refused
dataroomRefused.description: Bidder A asks for the customers' names. Provisa refuses: no customer name is granted to bidder_a, and neither are the CRM's business and deal names. Had the analyst named bidder B's role, which they do not hold, the request would be refused too, and recorded in the org's security trail as role probing.

dataroomBidderB.title: Now as bidder B
dataroomBidderB.description: Bidder B's clean team holds its own role, bidder_b, granted the same room and ending on the same date. Neither bidder sees what the other asks.

dataroomBidderBCohorts.title: Cohorts, as bidder B
dataroomBidderBCohorts.description: Customers who first ordered in the first quarter of 2023, and how many still ordered in each quarter after, with what they spent. Retention, without a single customer.

dataroomSeller.title: Back to the seller
dataroomSeller.description: The seller acts as every role it holds again, to see what the bidders did.

dataroomAudit.title: What each bidder looked at
dataroomAudit.description: Every statement is audited: who ran it, as which role, the tables it read, whether it was answered and how many rows it returned. Here are the statements you just ran as bidder A and bidder B. The seller knows exactly what left the room.

dataroomExpiry.title: Access ends on the deal date
dataroomExpiry.description: The Users page lists each grant with its end date and its last use. After the deal date the grants are gone, removed by the schedule and recorded in the org's trail, and nothing more leaves the room.

dataroomRevoke.title: Ending a bidder's access at once
dataroomRevoke.description: A bidder that drops out loses access in one action: remove its grant, or the role itself. The next request is refused. The audit of everything it read stays.

dataroomRecap.title: What you saw
dataroomRecap.description: A data room with no exports: the seller's own systems, read in place, shown to each bidder as aggregates, profiles, quality scores, masked samples and records without identities. No customer identity leaves the room. Each bidder holds a role of its own, granted until the deal date, and every statement is audited.

testdataScenario.title: Three environments over one production database
testdataScenario.description: shop-db is a shop's production database: customers, products and orders. Teams need data to build and test against. Here one model serves three environments. prod is the real rows, the source of truth, and nobody builds against it. preprod is production's own data with every sensitive column faked, for final testing. dev is generated from production's profile and holds nothing real, for everyday building.

testdataTables.title: The model says which columns are faked
testdataTables.description: On customers, the name, email, city and sign-up date each declare a fake, and so does the customer number: an identifier, and the sign-up date a quasi-identifier that could single someone out. Region, products, orders and amounts declare none, so they stay real. Which columns to fake is the operator's choice, made once in the model.

testdataCoverage.title: The steward checks coverage
testdataCoverage.description: Before pre-prod existed, the coverage check listed every sensitive column and whether a fake covers it. Here customers.email has none. A Test (fake) environment refuses to open, and refuses every read, while a sensitive column has no fake. Once the steward declares one, the column is covered.

testdataCoverageNow.title: Every sensitive column is covered
testdataCoverageNow.description: The same check, read now from the model: each sensitive column, its tags, and whether a fake covers it. Every one is covered, so pre-prod opens and answers.

testdataProd.title: Production: the real rows
testdataProd.description: In prod you see the customers as they really are.

testdataProdAnswer.title: Production's answer
testdataProdAnswer.description: Revenue by region and category, from the real orders.

testdataToPreprod.title: Switch to pre-prod
testdataToPreprod.description: Environments are branches of one model, as in git. Next, the switcher in the header moves to preprod, a Test (fake) environment.

testdataPreprod.title: Pre-prod: production's rows, identities faked
testdataPreprod.description: The same customers, read in preprod. Each name, email, city, sign-up date and customer number is a fake, computed as the row is read. The region is real. Pre-prod reads production's own data through Provisa, and the only identity that connects to production's stores is Provisa's own. Nothing is copied out.

testdataPreprodAnswer.title: The totals are production's
testdataPreprodAnswer.description: The same view in preprod gives exactly production's revenue by region and category. Every real row, volume and edge case is there for final testing. The customer number is faked the same way on customers and on orders, so the joins still match.

testdataPreprodAsAnalyst.title: No role lifts the fakes
testdataPreprodAsAnalyst.description: As analyst, or as any other role, pre-prod's sensitive columns read as fakes. No grant, mask or role shows the real values in a Test (fake) environment.

testdataToDev.title: Switch to dev
testdataToDev.description: Next, the switcher moves to dev, a Test (synthetic) environment.

testdataDev.title: Dev: generated, nothing real
testdataDev.description: Every row in dev was generated from production's profile: the same columns, value shapes and spread, and none of the real rows. This is also the answer when even pre-prod's real rows can't leave production's boundary: give testers a synthetic copy.

testdataDevAnswer.title: Same shape, different numbers
testdataDevAnswer.description: The same view in dev. The regions and categories are the ones production has, and the totals are close to production's without being its numbers.

testdataDevGraphql.title: Keys still join
testdataDevGraphql.description: Each order with the customer who placed it, through the relationship. Keys were generated to line up across tables, so every API reads dev as a consistent dataset.

testdataReport.title: How close the copy is
testdataReport.description: The generation report compares each generated table with the production profile it was drawn from, column by column: distributions, null rates, distinct values and how columns move together. It shows how close dev is to production, without showing production.

testdataToProd.title: Back to production
testdataToProd.description: Next, the switcher returns to prod.

testdataDone.title: What you saw
testdataDone.description: One model, three environments. Prod holds the real rows. Pre-prod reads them with every sensitive column faked, for every role. Dev is generated from production's profile and holds nothing real. Fakes are declared once per column, and an environment that would show a sensitive column unfaked refuses to open.

churnprodScenario.title: What this demo is
churnprodScenario.description: The churn demo's data scientist trained a scikit-learn model on the customers' usage to find who is about to cancel. Here that model goes to production. It ships as a Python package, and it scores every customer you may see, under the same rules as any table.

churnprodPackage.title: The model, as a source
churnprodPackage.description: The model's package is a source. It carries the fitted model and a lockfile that pins scikit-learn.

churnprodColumns.title: Columns from the function's types
churnprodColumns.description: churn_risk is a table because its docstring says @table. Its columns are the fields of the RiskRow it returns. Its parameters are its arguments, the customer and each feature the model was trained on.

churnprodJoin.title: The join that feeds the model
churnprodJoin.description: This relationship joins each customer to the model's score, so a join over customers scores every one of them.

churnprodAtRisk.title: The at-risk list
churnprodAtRisk.description: Every current customer, scored by the model and ranked by risk, with the reasons that raise each score most. It is one SQL statement over a view, and the model is called inside it.

churnprodAnalyst.title: Now as the analyst
churnprodAnalyst.description: The analyst reads the same list, as the churn demo's analyst reads its features.

churnprodMasked.title: Scores, emails masked
churnprodMasked.description: The scores are the same. The email addresses are masked, because the analyst's mask applies to the list as it applies to the customers' table.

churnprodRegional.title: Now as the EU account team
churnprodRegional.description: The EU account team looks after the customers billed in the EU.

churnprodRegionalRows.title: Its region's rows only
churnprodRegionalRows.description: Only EU customers are listed. The row rule sits on churn_risk itself, and a rule on a code table applies to the rows its code returns.

churnprodNode.title: The Node twin
churnprodNode.description: Here is the same model in JavaScript. Its fitted coefficients were exported from Python, and it is registered as a Node source beside the Python one. Each customer gets the same score from both.

churnprodRecap.title: What you saw
churnprodRecap.description: A data scientist's model went to production with no service of its own to run. Its package is pinned. A join feeds its function, which reads as a table, and the masks and row rules every table has govern what it returns. SQL, GraphQL and every other way in read it the same way.

worldcupIntro.title: Four public sources, one World Cup
worldcupIntro.description: Who has won the World Cup, and from which confederation? The answer is spread over public data: Wikipedia's list of finals and its confederation articles, and two Kaggle datasets of every World Cup match and every international goal. Each source names countries its own way. Wikipedia writes West Germany, Kaggle writes Germany FR, and the confederations' member tables write Germany. This tour sources the data, makes the names agree with a short Python function, and queries the result as one governed graph.

worldcupWikipedia.title: Wikipedia, registered in minutes
worldcupWikipedia.description: This is a Wikipedia source. Its crawl reads seven pages: the List of FIFA World Cup finals and the articles of the six confederations. Each data table on those pages becomes a table named by its page and its caption, so the finals are list_of_fifa_world_cup_finals__list_of_fifa_world_cup_finals. A public source is governed like any internal database, with the same roles, grants and masks. Set a refresh interval and these sources stay current on their own. This demo reads a fixed snapshot, so every visitor sees the same answers.

worldcupFinals.title: The finals, as Wikipedia lists them
worldcupFinals.description: Every final from 1930 to 2026, with the winners and runners-up by the names of their day. Wikipedia lists the 1954, 1974 and 1990 titles under West Germany and the 2014 title under Germany.

worldcupKaggle.title: Kaggle datasets arrive as tables
worldcupKaggle.description: This is a Kaggle source: the FIFA World Cup dataset, with every tournament, match and player appearance from 1930 to 2014. Each of its files arrives as a table. A second Kaggle source holds every international goal since 1916. Like the Wikipedia tables, they are public data, registered in minutes and governed like any internal database.

worldcupMatches.title: Matches by the names of their day
worldcupMatches.description: Kaggle writes West Germany as Germany FR and East Germany as German DR. A few of its names carry stray markup from the file, such as rn">Republic of Ireland. The file's blank lines are kept as rows with no values, as the dataset has them.

worldcupDisagree.title: The names disagree
worldcupDisagree.description: Counted by the names Wikipedia writes, Germany has one title and West Germany three, as if they were two countries. Kaggle writes the same team as Germany FR, so a join on names between the sources misses those titles too.

worldcupFunction.title: The function is the table
worldcupFunction.description:
country_alias is a Python source, and this function is the table every cross-source relationship joins through. It receives each team name the sources write, asks an LLM which FIFA member the name stands for, with a key from the organization's vault, and returns the member's name and FIFA code. It runs again on its refresh interval, so a new name is matched as it appears.
def country_alias(name: str) -> list[Alias]:
    """The FIFA member a team's name stands for: West Germany and Germany FR are Germany.

    @table
    """
    reply = anthropic.Anthropic().messages.create(
        model="claude-sonnet-5-5",
        max_tokens=2000,
        output_config={"effort": "low", "format": {"type": "json_schema", "schema": ANSWER}},
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": ASK + name}],
    )
    match = json.loads(next(b.text for b in reply.content if b.type == "text"))
    return [Alias(name, match["canonical_country"], match["fifa_code"])]

worldcupAlias.title: Every name, matched and reviewed
worldcupAlias.description: These are the names that differ from their member's name. Germany FR and West Germany are Germany, Zaire is DR Congo and the Soviet Union is Russia. Each match was reviewed before this demo froze it, and 27 of the 237 were corrected. A team whose results passed to no member keeps its own name: East Germany stays East Germany, so its 1974 match against West Germany is not Germany against Germany.

worldcupJunction.title: A relationship through the function
worldcupJunction.description: WON joins a confederation's member to the finals it won through country_alias. The member's FIFA code finds every name it stands for, and each name finds its finals. RUNNER_UP, PLAYED_HOME, PLAYED_AWAY and SCORED join the same way.

worldcupGraph.title: Every title in one graph
worldcupGraph.description: Each member links to the finals it won, under whatever name it won them. Germany's node holds 1954, 1974, 1990 and 2014.

worldcupByConfederation.title: Grouped by confederation
worldcupByConfederation.description: Grouped by confederation, UEFA's members hold 13 titles and CONMEBOL's hold 10. No other confederation has won a final.

worldcupSql.title: The same model in SQL
worldcupSql.description: The same join in SQL counts each member's titles through country_alias. Brazil leads with five, and Germany and Italy have four each.

worldcupGraphql.title: And in GraphQL
worldcupGraphql.description: In GraphQL each final has a winner field through country_alias, so 1954, 1974 and 1990 read West Germany beside the member they stand for: Germany, GER.

worldcupRecap.title: Recap
worldcupRecap.description: Public data from Wikipedia and Kaggle, sourced in minutes and governed like any internal database, made to agree by about ten lines of Python and queried as one graph. The function's matches were reviewed, so the graph counts every title once, under the right member.

cloudpolicyScenario.title: What this demo is
cloudpolicyScenario.description: Your security policy says every disk attached to a virtual machine uses a customer-managed key. You lead security, and you review that across Azure, AWS and Google Cloud from what is already recorded. The first source is the cloud inventory. It lists every machine and disk in the three clouds, with the key each disk is encrypted with.

cloudpolicyIncidents.title: The incidents
cloudpolicyIncidents.description: The second source is the security team's ServiceNow incidents. Each one names the disk it is about as its configuration item, and it cites the policy section it is filed under. An exception is an incident in the Policy exception category.

cloudpolicyReader.title: The policy, read by code
cloudpolicyReader.description: The policy itself is a web page. This Python package ships with the page and reads it into a row for each control. Its function is a table, so the policy joins the rest of the model.

cloudpolicyPolicy.title: The policy as rows
cloudpolicyPolicy.description: Here is every control of the policy, read from its HTML with its heading, its clause and the day it took effect. Section 4.2 is the disk-encryption control under review.

cloudpolicySearch.title: The policy, searched by meaning
cloudpolicySearch.description: A search by meaning finds the control about disk encryption even when your words differ from the clause's.

cloudpolicyModel.title: One model across three clouds
cloudpolicyModel.description: Each disk names the machine it is attached to. This relationship joins disks to machines in Azure, AWS and Google Cloud alike.

cloudpolicyCites.title: Incidents tied to clauses
cloudpolicyCites.description: Each incident cites a policy section. This relationship joins it to the clause it cites, so an incident filed under the wrong section shows up.

cloudpolicyViolations.title: The policy as a view
cloudpolicyViolations.description: Section 4.2 is written as a view. It lists every attached disk whose key the cloud manages, beside the machine the disk is on.

cloudpolicyReview.title: The daily review
cloudpolicyReview.description: The daily review classifies each attached disk by the policy's rules. A disk without a customer-managed key may be covered by an exception in date. If it is not, its incident is within its deadline or past it, closed with the disk still not compliant, or never filed.

cloudpolicyTrigger.title: The daily trigger
cloudpolicyTrigger.description: Each morning a scheduled trigger runs the review and writes the day's rows to the review history. It writes through the same governed pipeline as any statement, under its role's write grant.

cloudpolicyTrend.title: Fourteen days of history
cloudpolicyTrend.description: The history the trigger keeps shows the violations day by day. Disks drop out as their incidents are fixed, and a new violation shows up the day it appears.

cloudpolicyPollyViolators.title: Ask Polly who breaks the control
cloudpolicyPollyViolators.description: Polly reads the same governed model you do. It names the disks without a customer-managed key and the section that requires one.

cloudpolicyPollyExceptions.title: Exceptions still in date
cloudpolicyPollyExceptions.description: An exception lasts 90 days under section 4.3. Polly finds the disks it still covers.

cloudpolicyPollyWrongControl.title: Incidents under the wrong section
cloudpolicyPollyWrongControl.description: Some incidents cite a section other than the control they are about, and one cites a section the policy withdrew.

cloudpolicyPollyUnchecked.title: Controls nothing checks
cloudpolicyPollyUnchecked.description: The policy has controls that no check enforces. Polly compares the policy with the checks the team runs, and it can draft a view for a steward to add.

cloudpolicyAuditor.title: Now as the auditor
cloudpolicyAuditor.description: The auditor reads every account in every cloud.

cloudpolicyOpen.title: Everything the review flags
cloudpolicyOpen.description: Here is every disk the review flags, for every team.

cloudpolicyAppTeam.title: Now as the payments team
cloudpolicyAppTeam.description: The payments team reads its own resources and incidents only.

cloudpolicyAppTeamRows.title: Its own rows only
cloudpolicyAppTeamRows.description: The same statement returns only the payments team's disks. The row rules sit on the inventory and the incidents, and every view built on them applies them.

cloudpolicyDashboard.title: The compliance dashboard
cloudpolicyDashboard.description: Superset reads the same views through Provisa's Postgres protocol. Here is its compliance dashboard, with the violations by control.

cloudpolicyRecap.title: What you saw
cloudpolicyRecap.description: You reviewed one policy across three clouds from what was already recorded. The policy is a table, read by code from its own page, and each incident joins the clause it cites. A daily trigger keeps the history, and each role reads only what its rules allow, in SQL, in Polly and in Superset.

bankingScenario.title: End-of-day reporting, ledger left in place
bankingScenario.description: A bank reports its totals at every business day's 18:00 close, and restates a past day when a correction arrives later. The usual way first copies the ledger into the warehouse. This demo does not. Watch four things as you go. What the reporting costs to compute. How much data the warehouse holds, and so how much it must govern. Whether the dashboard, BI and an agent give the same answer. And what it costs to change the decision later.

bankingJoin.title: From a total to its postings
bankingJoin.description: Each total carries one key made of its day, branch, product and currency. This relationship follows that key to the postings that carry it, read live from the ledger. The drill-down needs no copy either.

bankingRecap.title: What you saw
bankingRecap.description: The end-of-day totals were computed at the ledger, and the warehouse paid only for what it keeps. The warehouse holds totals and never postings, so there is no second copy of the ledger to govern. The dashboard, BI and the agent read one declared relationship and gave the same numbers. And if keeping the ledger home turns out wrong, a two-line placement change moves it while nothing that reads it changes. Choose lean now: being wrong costs two lines, not a project.

bankingLedger.title: The ledger stays home
bankingLedger.description: The transaction table is homed in the ledger region and never replicated. No copy of a posting ever lands in the warehouse, and every query over the table runs in the ledger. The end-of-day totals and the drill-downs come off the warehouse's bill, for modest compute in the ledger. Only the totals reach the warehouse, plus the postings a drill-down shows, in passing. The cost is lower and the footprint smaller.

bankingVersions.title: A correction is a new row
bankingVersions.description: The ledger never changes a posting. A correction is a new row with the same transaction id, and it keeps the business date. Three mappings tell Provisa so. The business key is transaction_id, the valid time is business_date and the recorded time is updated_at. Anything built on the table can then be read as of a day, or as it was recorded at a time.

bankingCompute.title: What the ledger needs
bankingCompute.description: This works when the ledger's side has the compute to run the end-of-day GROUP BY. Replicating is not free for it either. Every changed row has to be found, read in full and shipped, and aggregating in place is often lighter. With high volumes, reports that read totals and an occasional drill-down, keeping the ledger home tends to win. The declaration lets you choose either way.

bankingCloses.title: Built at each close
bankingCloses.description: The end-of-day totals are a view materialized in the warehouse on the bank's calendar, which closes at 18:00 London time. The view is one GROUP BY over the ledger's one table, so its build runs whole at the ledger and only the grouped rows come back. It inherits the ledger's versions and needs no history settings of its own. Each day was recorded at its own close. 1 and 2 October were recorded again later, when their restatements arrived.

bankingAsOps.title: As operations
bankingAsOps.description: The next query runs as operations, who drill into postings under the ledger's own rules. They see no posting to a staff account, and every counterparty is withheld.

bankingDashboard.title: The dashboard, over GraphQL
bankingDashboard.description: London's totals for 1 October, each with the postings behind it nested inside. One request reads the totals from the warehouse and the postings from the ledger, joined along the relationship you just saw.

bankingAsAnalyst.title: As a reporting analyst
bankingAsAnalyst.description: The SQL that follows runs as the bank's reporting analysts. They read the end-of-day totals and the five ledger columns the totals are built from: business date, branch, product, currency and amount. They never see an account, a counterparty or a holder.

bankingDay.title: One day's totals
bankingDay.description: 1 October as it stands now. For each branch, product and currency you see what came in, what went out and the net. A BI tool connected over pgwire runs this same SQL.

bankingAsReported.title: As reported at the close
bankingAsReported.description: As recorded is now set to 1 October's close. A BI tool does the same with SET provisa.as_recorded on its pgwire session. As recorded filters the transactions on updated_at and the daily totals on each day's close, so you see the figures the bank reported that evening.

bankingReported.title: What was reported
bankingReported.description: The corporate totals for 1 and 2 October, as reported at 1 October's close. London's GBP total still carries the payment that was later reversed. 2 October had not closed yet, so it has no figures.

bankingAsRestated.title: As restated since
bankingAsRestated.description: As recorded moves to 12 October's close, the last of the thirty days. By then the reversal entered on 6 October and the late trade entered on 7 October have both been recorded.

bankingRestated.title: What it says now
bankingRestated.description: The same SQL. London's 1 October total no longer carries the reversed payment, and Edinburgh's 2 October USD total now includes the late trade. The versions reported at each close are kept beside the restated ones, and recorded_at shows when each was recorded.

bankingAsOpsSql.title: Back to operations
bankingAsOpsSql.description: The explorer now runs as operations, still as recorded at 12 October's close.

bankingPostings.title: The postings behind a total
bankingPostings.description: London's corporate GBP postings for 1 October, read live from the ledger. The recalled payment appears as its latest version, reversed. Its counterparty is withheld, like every other, and a posting to a staff account would not appear. The ledger's rules apply to the drill-down wherever it is read from.

bankingAgent.title: The agent's answer
bankingAgent.description: An agent connected over MCP reads the same model. Polly answers this question from the same end-of-day totals the dashboard and BI read, so it names the same branch.

bankingChange.title: Changing your mind costs two lines
bankingChange.description: Suppose volumes outgrow the ledger's compute. Set this table's region to warehouse and its replicate setting to Always, and the ledger is replicated into the warehouse. That is a two-line placement change, and every query, dashboard, BI view and agent answers as before. Built by hand, the same move means new pipelines, a backfill, rewritten aggregation and versioning, repointed reports and a second set of access rules. Then come reconciliation testing, audit and lineage checks, architecture and security review, and a change board. Here the change is a two-line reviewed diff, so testing, audit and architecture review a diff, not a migration.

bankingAsAdmin.title: Back as the administrator
bankingAsAdmin.description: The dashboard is what operations sees. The rest of the tour is back as the administrator, and each statement that follows names the role it runs as.

status.waiting: Waiting for this page to finish loading…
status.stuck: This step is taking longer than expected. The page may still be loading.

weblogs.title: The web shop's logs
weblogs.summary: Which pages of a web shop are slow, and which SQL makes them slow? See the shop's sources, the tables they become, the join between its two logs, and the answer in SQL and over REST.

sonnets.title: Shakespeare's sonnets
sonnets.summary: The 154 sonnets embedded, searched by meaning and grown into a graph: the themes they share and the lines where Shakespeare echoes himself.

files.title: Instant data lake
files.summary: A city's open-data files read in place as one catalog: which neighborhoods have the most complaints near active construction?

reviews.title: Product reviews
reviews.summary: An electronics shop's catalog, reviews and purchases in MongoDB, Elasticsearch and Neo4j, joined on the product: which products do reviews say the battery dies on, and what else did their buyers buy?

insurance.title: Property exposure and hazard risk
insurance.summary: Where is a property insurer's exposure concentrated against hazard risk? Its own policies, joined by county to FEMA, wildfire and storm data, answer it in SQL, GraphQL and REST.

quality.title: Data you can trust
quality.summary: A chain of shops' sales feed, refined from bronze to silver and gold by checked materialized views. Landing a batch is all it takes, and a batch that fails a check never reaches silver.

insider.title: Insider review
insider.summary: A bank checks its outbound mail against the watch list of deals in discussion, and for customer data. Everything is ranked in one review queue that a first-level reviewer works through without ever seeing the list.

vulnerabilities.title: Exploited vulnerabilities in our code
vulnerabilities.summary: Which exploited vulnerabilities are in a software company's code, and how far past CISA's due date are they? Its Dependabot alerts, joined by CVE to the NVD and CISA's catalog of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities, answer it.

testdata.title: Test data
testdata.summary: A shop's production database in three environments: the real rows in prod, production's rows with every sensitive column faked in pre-prod, and generated rows with nothing real in dev.

streaming.title: Live order stream
streaming.summary: A coffee shop's orders arrive live on Kafka and are joined to its catalog. A view of the busiest regions over the last five minutes refreshes with every batch, answers in SQL, GraphQL and REST, can be cached, and can be watched with a subscription.

profiling.title: What is actually in this data?
profiling.summary: An acquired company's customers and orders, profiled by the built-in Data Profiler: nulls, ranges, formats, plausible types and duplicates, landed as governed tables and read in SQL, GraphQL and REST.

opioids.title: Opioid settlement funds and overdose deaths
opioids.summary: Which counties have the most overdose deaths for the treatment their opioid settlement money pays for? A fund's allocations, joined by county to CDC, Census and federal spending data, answer a local government's question.

datavault.title: Data vault
datavault.summary: A data vault declared over an order system and a CRM. The engine builds and refreshes its hubs, links and satellites as rows arrive, personal data is masked in the satellites, and one point-in-time query shows what was known about a customer, from which source, and when.

agriculture.title: Weather and crop insurance losses
agriculture.summary: Does weather explain the losses in a crop insurer's portfolio? Its own farms, policies and claims, joined by county and crop year to the USDA's losses by cause, NOAA's weather and NASS's yields, answer it in SQL, GraphQL and REST.

retail.title: One group, two regions
retail.summary: A retail group with an EU and a US subsidiary run as one business under GDPR: EU data stays in the EU, group reporting reads it pseudonymised, and access, erasure, insider review and audit are each one query.

provisioning.title: Provisioning datasets to downstream teams
provisioning.summary: How do downstream teams get big datasets as soon as they're ready? Feeds land from Kafka, datasets refresh as they land, and each team is told on Kafka and pulls over Arrow Flight as of that moment.

pharma.title: Drug shortage and recall risk
pharma.summary: Which of a hospital pharmacy's products face shortage or recall risk? Its formulary and stock, joined to FDA's shortages and recalls and Medicaid's prescriptions, answer it in SQL, GraphQL and REST.

storefront.title: One model, app and BI
storefront.summary: An app's order-history screen and a BI dashboard read one model of PostgreSQL, MongoDB and a REST service, under the same relationships and rules.

hasuramigration.title: Moving a Hasura app
hasuramigration.summary: A Hasura v2 storefront imported in one step, its queries reshaped once, then joined to the sales team's Salesforce accounts under the same rules.

reproduce.title: Reproduce a report
reproduce.summary: A regulator's two questions about a bank's exposure report: where a figure came from, and what the report said when it was filed, untouched by a correction since. Lineage, as-of replay and the audit log answer both.

churn.title: Predict customer churn
churn.summary: Which customers are about to cancel? Their governed, masked features are read into pandas in the browser, and a scikit-learn model is trained on them in the notebook that ships with the demo.

dataroom.title: Data room for a sale
dataroom.summary: A retailer selling itself gives each bidder's clean team governed, time-limited access to its own systems with no exports: aggregates, profiles and masked samples, and no customer identity leaves the room.

churnprod.title: Churn risk in production
churnprod.summary: The churn demo's scikit-learn model in production. Its Python package is a source, and its function is a table that scores every customer in a join, with masks and row rules applied to what it returns.

worldcup.title: World Cup, one graph
worldcup.summary: Wikipedia's and Kaggle's World Cup data disagree on country names. A short Python function matches every name with an LLM, and the public sources become one governed graph.

cloudpolicy.title: Cloud policy review
cloudpolicy.summary: A security policy reviewed across Azure, AWS and Google Cloud. The cloud inventory, the ServiceNow incidents and the policy itself, read from its web page by code, are one model, and a daily trigger keeps the review's history.

banking.title: EOD reporting without copying the ledger
banking.summary: A bank's end-of-day totals, built at each close straight from a ledger that is never copied to the warehouse, read as reported and as restated, with the same answer over GraphQL, SQL and an agent.
